prize_parts.citation: For the detection of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory and the opening of neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: B043 is the discovery on the shortlist that most clearly came from clues in nature rather than from an elegant idea. A kilometre-cubed detector in Antarctic ice found a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos in 2013, the 2017-18 association with TXS 0506+056 gave a first source, and the Galactic-plane result in 2023 added a second, independent kind of evidence. That is a new observational window of the sort the committee has repeatedly rewarded, and it speaks directly to where cosmic rays come from. The credit structure is also workable: Halzen conceived and drove IceCube and its AMANDA precursor, while Spiering was a founding figure of neutrino telescopy from Baikal through AMANDA to IceCube. Having listened to colleagues, I keep B043 first, but I hold it with less certainty than in my opening ballot, mainly on the attribution question.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the source identification is still thin: TXS 0506+056 is a single-source association at modest significance, the Galactic-plane map is a diffuse result, and most of the diffuse flux is still unexplained. Attribution is also soft. IceCube is a collaboration of hundreds, DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA all preceded it, and a two-name prize necessarily leaves out people with real claims. If the committee cannot be satisfied through outside expert reports about who was decisive, B006 is the cleaner prize and B004 the more mature one.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B043 first as a detector-driven opening of a new window, with Halzen as conceiver and Spiering as founding figure of neutrino telescopy, while noting that the TXS 0506+056 association is a single-source result of roughly 3 sigma and that the Baikal and AMANDA pioneers and other leaders could be argued for.
responses.response: I agree with Pearce on the nature of the discovery and share the caveat on TXS 0506+056. I would answer it by resting the citation on the detection of the astrophysical flux, which was seen independently in several channels, rather than on source identification. That also meets Mehlig's point below. Where I am less certain than Pearce is attribution: as Secretary I would want the outside reports to say specifically whether Spiering's role in Baikal and AMANDA was decisive or whether another early leader should stand beside Halzen.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B043 only seventh because the diffuse flux is statistically solid but the source identification is still developing, so the astrophysical interpretation is still maturing, and he notes that Baikal, AMANDA and other pioneers complicate a two-person credit.
responses.response: Mehlig is right that the astronomy is unfinished, but I do not think that makes the discovery premature. The Nobel tradition does not wait for a field to answer every question; it asks whether a new window has been opened and independently confirmed. The flux has been confirmed, and the 2023 Galactic-plane result is a second, independent line of evidence. I accept his attribution point without reservation, and it is the real obstacle for B043. His other first choice, B009, is where I would press him in turn: the superconducting mechanism there is still debated, which is a larger maturity problem than the one he raises against IceCube.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B006 first as a textbook case of a measurement advance opening new physics, with the magic-wavelength idea from Katori and the 10^-18 performance from Ye, a clean two-person prize, and confirmation at the 10^-18 level by many laboratories.
responses.response: Kroll and Lindroth have moved me on B006. I ranked it sixth in my opening because the frequency-comb prize of 2005 made it look incremental, but a tenfold-plus gain in precision with new tests of relativity and constants is clean science of the kind I say I value. I would not call it a discovery in my sense, though, since no new phenomenon has yet appeared in the clock comparisons. It becomes more persuasive if the redefinition of the second or a search result is added to the case. I therefore rank it as my first alternative, not as a competitor to B043 in this round.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B004 first as a genuinely new state of matter, with Kane and Mele supplying the decisive theory and Molenkamp the HgTe experiment, while flagging that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction is left out.
responses.response: The Z2 classification is a deep idea and I am comfortable with it as my second alternative. My doubt is that the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio stitches a theory prize to a later experiment that was proposed by other theorists. If Zhang's death in 2018 removes one natural candidate, the committee is left rewarding a sequence whose logic was completed by people it cannot name. That is a harder attribution problem than the one Eriksson accepts, and the 2016 prize on topological phases adds an overlap issue. I would need to see an expert report on who really made the decisive step before I could rank it above B043.

uncertainties: Whether Spiering, or another early leader of AMANDA, Baikal or DUMAND, should stand beside Halzen is not settled by the openings and needs outside expert reports.
Whether the single-source TXS 0506+056 association and the Galactic-plane result are strong enough that the citation can rest on source identification, or only on the detection of the diffuse flux.
Whether the committee regards B006 as a discovery or as a precision-measurement advance, given the 2005 frequency-comb prize.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap in B004 can be bridged by a different choice of names within the allowed credited set.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. None of the shortlisted candidates is connected to Uppsala, my PhD supervisor David Gross, Thomas Van Riet or my other collaborators. My own work is in string theory and cosmology, which are not on this shortlist, so I am a non-expert on all eight.
